title: Topology Optimization: SIMP Method and Bracket Example
summary: Topology optimization explained: SIMP, compliance, filters and the OC update, with real MBB beam and L-bracket runs, manufacturing rules and tools.
body_markdown:
Topology optimization is a finite-element method that decides where material should go inside a design space. You give it the space, the loads, the supports and a material budget, and it removes material that carries little load until the stiffest layout for that budget is left. Size optimization only changes thicknesses, and shape optimization only moves existing boundaries. Topology optimization can also create holes, so it finds the layout itself.


This guide, for mechanical and CAE students who know basic FEA, explains the SIMP density method, filtering and the optimizer's update rule. We then run our own Python port of the 88-line MATLAB code on a beam and an L-bracket, and show how a result becomes a part you can make.

## What is topology optimization?


Topology optimization chooses the layout of material: how many members, where the holes are and how the load paths connect. Each element of a fixed mesh gets a design variable that says whether it holds material, and the optimizer changes those variables to improve an objective such as stiffness within a limit such as mass.


Engineers usually separate three kinds of structural optimization (Bendsøe and Sigmund, 2003):


Type What the optimizer changes What stays fixed Typical use


Size Thicknesses, cross-section areas, gauges The layout and the shape of every boundary Sheet gauges in a car body, rib thicknesses, truss member areas


Shape The position of existing boundaries (hole outlines, fillets) The number of holes and members Reducing a stress peak at a fillet or a hole edge


Topology Whether each point holds material, so holes can appear and members can merge Only the design space, loads and supports Concept layout of brackets, ribs and mounts


Size, shape and topology optimization on the same design space. The topology panel is our own optimized half MBB beam (120 x 40 elements, sensitivity filter).


In practice the three run in sequence. Topology optimization gives a concept, a designer rebuilds it in CAD, and size and shape optimization then fine-tune it. Airbus UK engineers used exactly this sequence in Altair's OptiStruct to design 13 droop-nose ribs for the A380 in a five-week programme (Krog, Tucker and Rollema).


The method goes back to Bendsøe and Kikuchi's 1988 homogenization paper; a year later Bendsøe proposed the simpler power-law material model that became SIMP.

## How do you topology-optimize a bracket?


Make the design space the envelope the bracket may occupy. Mark regions that must stay solid (bolt bosses, pin lugs) or empty (clearance for other parts), add loads and supports, choose a volume fraction and let the optimizer remove the rest. Then threshold, smooth and rebuild the result in CAD.


Our L-bracket adds passive (forced-empty) elements, as section 5 of the paper describes. It is a 100 x 100 element box with the top-right 60 x 60 square kept empty, leaving 6,400 design elements. The top of the vertical arm is clamped, and a downward unit load is shared by five nodes at the tip. We used 40% volume,


p


=


3


and a density filter of radius 3.


Our L-bracket: design space, optimized density field, and the same design cut to solid and void at the same 40% volume.


- The run converged in **359 iterations** , with compliance falling from 1,896.5 to **261.5** (86.2% lower).
- The vertical arm became two separate columns that act like a frame against the bending, and the horizontal arm became a triangulated truss.
- 30.4% of design elements finished grey. Cut at density 0.568, which keeps the volume at exactly 0.400, and re-analysed as pure solid and void, the design has a compliance of **205.2** , 21.5% lower than the grey value.


SIMP counts a grey element at


x


3


of its stiffness, so the optimizer's own compliance is not a physical number while grey remains. Report stiffness from a fresh FE run on the cleaned geometry, and check stress in that run too, because compliance says nothing about the stress peak at the inner corner.


## How do you turn a topology optimization result into a manufacturable part?


Treat the result as a concept, not a drawing: threshold the density field, smooth it, rebuild it as clean CAD, then re-analyse that CAD for stress, deflection, buckling and fatigue. Set the manufacturing process as a constraint before the optimization, not afterwards.


1. **Threshold.** Choose a density cut-off, as we did at 0.568. Heaviside projection filters (Guest et al., 2004; section 5 of the 88-line paper) push the optimizer itself to give black-and-white designs with a minimum member size, so the choice of threshold matters less.
2. **Smooth and fit.** The raw result is a staircase of elements. Altair Inspire, for example, smooths the result and then fits PolyNURBS surfaces to it so the geometry can be exported to CAD. Ansys's additive manufacturing workflow cleans up the optimized geometry in SpaceClaim and then validates it in Mechanical (Ansys help, 2024 R2); our[additive manufacturing course in Ansys SpaceClaim](https://skill-lync.com/mechanical-engineering-courses/additive-manufacturing-3dprinting-ansys-spaceclaim) covers that tool.
3. **Re-design in CAD.** Rebuild bosses, mating faces and holes to exact dimensions, add fillets, and use ordinary features so the part can be dimensioned and toleranced.
4. **Verify.** Check von Mises stress against the allowable for every load case, and buckling of slender members. Compliance optimization checks none of these.


Each process brings its own limits, and commercial tools let you set them as manufacturing constraints:


Process What limits the shape Constraint to set


Metal additive (powder bed) Overhangs need supports. Powder must drain from internal cavities. There is a minimum wall thickness. Overhang angle and build direction (Ansys AM Overhang Constraint), minimum member size


Casting and moulding The part must come out of the die. Walls should be uniform, and faces need draft. Draw direction (single or split die), no holes along the draw, minimum thickness


Machining The tool must reach every surface. Internal cavities and undercuts are expensive or impossible. Tool or pull-out direction, extrusion (constant cross-section)


Sheet metal The part is a formed sheet of constant thickness. Stamping constraint, or switch to size or bead optimization


**Minimum member size** matters most: without it the optimizer happily makes bars one element thick. OptiStruct's help recommends 3 to 12 times the average element size (6 to 24 mm on a 2 mm mesh) and warns that the control discourages small members without strictly forbidding them. The real limit comes from the process; GE's 2013 bracket challenge set a minimum wall of 0.050 in (1.27 mm) for printed titanium.


For printed parts, our[Design for AM chapter](https://skill-lync.com/books/additive-manufacturing#unit-16-dfam) covers overhangs, part consolidation and lattices, and our[additive manufacturing primer](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/the-fundamentals-of-additive-manufacturing) explains the processes.


## Where is topology optimization used in industry?


It is most common where mass is expensive, in aircraft structure, engine brackets and automotive parts. Published examples with numbers:


- **Airbus A380.** Airbus used topology optimization to redesign A380 components including the inboard fixed leading-edge ribs and fuselage door intercostals. Airbus UK's rib work was done in Altair's OptiStruct. A 2016 AIAA paper by Chin and Kennedy summarizes the weight savings as of the order of 103 kg per aircraft. The original papers are Krog et al. (2004) and Grihon et al. (2004).
- **Bombardier wingbox ribs.** The same AIAA paper reports that Bombardier used topology optimization in a passenger jet's wingbox ribs and cut the component's weight by 10%. The cited study was constrained to traditional design and manufacturing requirements.
- **GE jet engine bracket challenge (2013).** GE and GrabCAD asked the public to lighten a titanium engine bracket within its original envelope under four load cases. From nearly 700 entries in 56 countries, the winner cut the mass from 2,033 g to 327 g, nearly 84%. GE printed and load-tested the top ten; its own designers had used in-house optimization tools to predict the outcome (Carter et al., 2014).
- **General Motors seat bracket (2018).** With Autodesk's generative design, GM produced a seat bracket that is 40% lighter and 20% stronger than the original. It merges eight components into one 3D-printed part, chosen from more than 150 design options (Autodesk, 3 May 2018). It was a proof of concept, and it is an example of generative design, explained below.


## Which software is used for topology optimization?


The main commercial tools are Altair OptiStruct and Inspire, Ansys Mechanical, Abaqus with Tosca Structure, and Autodesk Fusion's generative design. They solve the same kind of FE-based problem as our code, at 3D scale, with manufacturing constraints and tools to turn the result into geometry.


Tool What it offers for topology optimization


Altair OptiStruct Solver-level topology, size and shape optimization. Its manufacturing controls include minimum and maximum member size, draw direction (single or split die, no-hole, stamping), extrusion, pattern repetition and symmetry. Altair has been part of Siemens since 26 March 2025.


Altair Inspire A designer-facing interface: optimize, smooth the result, fit PolyNURBS surfaces and export geometry to CAD.


Ansys Mechanical Structural Optimization with density-based, level-set and mixable-density topology methods. It has member-size, pull-out direction, extrusion and AM overhang constraints. Ansys has been part of Synopsys since 17 July 2025.


Abaqus with Tosca Structure Topology, shape, sizing and bead optimization, built on Abaqus (Dassault Systèmes SIMULIA).


Autodesk Fusion Generative design with manufacturing methods: unrestricted, additive (X+, Y+, Z+ build directions), 2.5-, 3- and 5-axis milling, 2-axis cutting and casting.


If you set up the study in Ansys, our guide to[choosing the right Ansys structural analysis](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/structural-analysis-in-ansys-guide-to-choosing-the-right-simulation-method) explains the static model that the Structural Optimization system sits on.


## What is the difference between topology optimization and generative design?


Topology optimization solves one well-defined problem and returns one optimized layout. Generative design wraps optimization in a design exploration: it runs many studies across materials, manufacturing methods and goals, and gives the engineer a set of candidate designs to compare, each already shaped for a process.


Topology optimization Generative design


Output One density or level-set field for one problem Many outcomes (GM's bracket study gave more than 150 options)


Inputs Design space, loads, supports, objective, constraint The same, plus a list of materials and manufacturing methods to explore


Geometry Element field that needs smoothing and CAD rebuild Usually returns smooth, editable geometry for each outcome


Engineer's role Set up the problem, interpret the result, redesign Set up the problem, then choose between trade-offs


Compute One optimization run (our 2D runs took seconds to minutes) Many optimizations; Fusion runs them as a cloud solve


Generative design builds on topology optimization, so learn the method first. Our article on[AI CAD tools](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/text-to-cad-ai-cad-copilots-mechanical-design) shows where generative design sits among newer AI-assisted tools.


## What are the limits of topology optimization?


The method finds a stiff layout for a given mass under the loads you specify, and its limits come from that same sentence.


- **Only the loads you give it.** A bracket optimized for one load case can be weak under another, so real studies combine several.
- **Stiffness is not strength.** Compliance minimization ignores stress peaks, fatigue and buckling. Stress-constrained formulations exist but are harder to solve.
- **Settings matter.** The result depends on penalty, filter radius, starting design and mesh; our two filters gave visibly different beams for the same problem.
- **Linear and static by default.** Contact, plasticity, large deflection and crash loads need special formulations or a different approach.
- **Cleanup changes the answer.** On our L-bracket the cut design was 21.5% stiffer than the grey number suggested, so always re-analyse the final geometry.


## How do you learn topology optimization?


Start with linear static FEA: meshing, boundary conditions and reading stress plots. Then run the 88-line code or a port and change one setting at a time (penalty, filter radius, mesh), and finally learn a commercial tool on a real bracket. A weak FE model gives a confident but wrong optimum.


Skill-Lync's[Pre-Graduate Program in Finite Element Analysis](https://skill-lync.com/mechanical-engineering-courses/pre-graduate-program-finite-element-analysis) builds the FEA base. The[Post Graduate Program in CAE](https://skill-lync.com/mechanical-engineering-courses/masters-cae) covers HyperMesh pre-processing for solvers including OptiStruct. Our[FEA book's meshing chapter](https://skill-lync.com/books/finite-element-analysis#unit-16-meshing) explains the mesh-independence checks this method depends on, and the[CAE engineer salary page](https://skill-lync.com/salaries/cae-engineer) shows what the role pays in India.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is topology optimization the same as FEA?


No. FEA analyses a design you already have. Topology optimization runs FEA again and again inside a loop (53 to 400 times in our runs) and changes the material layout between runs. FEA is the engine and topology optimization is the search around it.


### Why is the penalty p usually 3?


A penalty of 3 makes intermediate densities poor value, so the result is mostly solid and void. It is still smooth enough for the optimizer to make progress. The 88-line paper calls


p


=


3


typical. Higher values make the result more black and white but make local optima more likely.


### Can I do topology optimization for free?


Yes, for learning. The 88-line MATLAB code is free from DTU's TopOpt group for education, and a Python port needs only NumPy and SciPy. For commercial tools, check each vendor's current student terms.


### Does topology optimization only work for 3D-printed parts?


No. Additive manufacturing can make organic shapes directly, but cast and machined parts are optimized too. You set draw-direction, extrusion or member-size constraints so the result suits the process. Airbus's A380 ribs and Bombardier's wingbox rib are both examples from conventionally made aircraft structure.
